The former speculative artifact contract is withdrawn.\n\n## **D.1 Current canonical home**\n\nSection 8.13 is the single current PF12 home for stateless or no-database BodyGraph export, compatibility export, and optional run-bundle evidence families. This appendix does not defer, redefine, or duplicate that contract.\n\n## **D.2 Boundary and nonclaims**\n\nThis appendix defines no artifact fields, schemas, paths, commands, transport surfaces, CI jobs, acceptance tokens, QA procedures, or implementation requirements. Its presence does not establish implementation, adoption, execution, QA PASS, acceptance, or repository conformance.\n\n",
    "391bf7d2eb51022e22edb69b90a2ed6eaa63f621dedcf817513c2ae1a0c77e24": "# 7 Phases of Alchemical Engineering\n\nUse this 7‑phase alchemy map as a way to name *what mode you’re in* with a product: are you burning away old assumptions, opening options, narrowing, integrating, letting it live with users, refining, or solidifying? The power is in not mixing modes—once you know the phase, you can choose sane practices, expectations, and decision styles for that moment in the product’s life.\n\n---\n\n### **Hermetic Overlay (very compact)**\n\n* **Ψ (Spirit)** – vision & meaning of the product (“why”).\n\n* **Λ (Mind)** – models, architecture, strategy (“how”).\n\n* **Σ (Body)** – code, processes, campaigns, org (“what”).\n\nEach phase transforms all three, but below I’ll focus on concrete Σ‑level actions.\n\n---\n\n## **1\\. Calcination – Burn down to the real problem**\n\n**Definition**  \n Breaking down existing beliefs, plans, and assets until only the non‑negotiable essentials remain. It feels harsh: assumptions, vanity projects, and comforting illusions get “burned off.”\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Audit existing code, systems, and tools; call out what’s brittle, obsolete, or blocking.\n\n* Run spike prototypes purely to invalidate risky technical assumptions.\n\n* Stop “feature accumulation”; ruthlessly kill half‑baked ideas and zombie branches.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Pre‑mortems: “If this product failed in 18 months, what killed it?”\n\n* Surface hard constraints (regulation, costs, talent, runway) instead of hiding them.\n\n* Challenge org habits: meetings, approvals, and roles that don’t serve the new product.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Listen for raw, unfiltered customer pain; treat criticism as fuel.\n\n* Kill vague value props and buzzword decks; insist on one sharp problem statement.\n\n* Drop channels that only serve vanity metrics (impressions, likes) with no learning.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Define the *core problem* and success criteria; decide what game you are refusing to play.\n\n* Explicitly list “what this product will NOT do” to set boundaries.\n\n* Decide whether this initiative survives at all; sometimes Calcination ends with a kill.\n\n---\n\n## **2\\. Dissolution – Melt into possibilities**\n\n**Definition**  \n Once the rigid shell is burned away, you “dissolve” what’s left into many options: open exploration, research, and ambiguity. Things are fluid on purpose.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Build quick, ugly prototypes to explore solutions, not to ship.\n\n* Experiment with different tech stacks or architectures without committing.\n\n* Pair design \\+ engineering in low‑fidelity flows and clickable mockups.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Keep the team structure light and flexible; minimal process, maximum exploration.\n\n* Run discovery sessions across departments (sales, support, finance) to surface constraints.\n\n* Try different ways of working (Kanban vs sprints, async vs sync) in “trial mode.”\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Conduct broad customer interviews and shadow sessions; collect language and stories.\n\n* Test many rough positioning angles (landing pages, ads, pitch scripts) for signal.\n\n* Explore multiple potential segments/use cases instead of picking one prematurely.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Map the problem space: adjacent jobs‑to‑be‑done, alternative solutions, substitutes.\n\n* Explore multiple business models (usage‑based, seat, freemium, services‑plus‑product).\n\n* Treat this as a divergent phase: postpone “final answer” decisions.\n\n---\n\n## **3\\. Separation – Filter, sort, and choose**\n\n**Definition**  \n You filter the fluid mass: separate signal from noise, core from peripheral, must‑have from nice‑to‑have. Options are winnowed.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Evaluate prototypes; choose the primary architecture and tech stack.\n\n* Define clear system boundaries and interfaces (APIs, modules, services).\n\n* Slice the backlog into *MVP vs later*; mark experiments as “keep,” “archive,” or “delete.”\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Decide core roles for this product (PM, tech lead, design, data, GTM owner).\n\n* Choose a minimal set of processes (e.g., sprint reviews, incident handling) to formalize.\n\n* Select a handful of key metrics (not 30\\) that will drive decisions.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Pick a primary persona and primary use case; stop trying to talk to everyone.\n\n* Select 1–2 main acquisition channels to learn deeply.\n\n* Drop weak messages that tested poorly; keep the one that actually moved people.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Define the MVP scope and acceptance criteria; commit to what “done for v1” means.\n\n* Choose a go‑to‑market motion (product‑led, sales‑led, partner‑led) instead of blending all.\n\n* Decide which future directions are deliberately *not* pursued this cycle.\n\n---\n\n## **4\\. Conjunction – Combine into a working whole**\n\n**Definition**  \n Previously separated elements—requirements, designs, architectures, and plans—are recombined into a coherent, functioning product. Integration becomes the main work.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Build the MVP end‑to‑end, integrating services, UI, and data flows.\n\n* Establish CI/CD, shared environments, and integration tests.\n\n* Resolve dependencies across teams; unify logging, monitoring, and error handling.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Create a cross‑functional product squad (eng, design, PM, data, GTM).\n\n* Align cadences: product planning, engineering sprints, and GTM timelines.\n\n* Stand up operational basics: support inbox, on‑call rotation, incident playbooks.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Align messaging across website, deck, docs, and sales scripts to tell one story.\n\n* Coordinate launch readiness: pricing page, FAQs, onboarding emails, demo flows.\n\n* Integrate feedback loops from sales/support back into the product team.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Articulate a single, cohesive product thesis (“who we serve, with what, and why now”).\n\n* Align pricing, packaging, and feature tiers to that thesis.\n\n* Plan the initial release train: v1, v1.1, and what happens in the first 90–180 days.\n\n---\n\n## **5\\. Fermentation – Let the product live (and rot a bit)**\n\n**Definition**  \n The product meets real users. Their use, abuse, and feedback introduce “new life” that changes the product. Some things spoil; new value cultures.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Ship to early adopters / beta and watch real usage patterns.\n\n* Patch critical bugs quickly; prioritize stability over new features.\n\n* Instrument the product (events, logs, traces) to observe behaviour, not just opinions.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Stand up a basic customer support loop: ticketing, SLAs, escalation paths.\n\n* Capture qualitative insights from support/success in a structured way.\n\n* Start using operational data (churn, activation, support load) in planning.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Run early‑access, beta, or design‑partner programs.\n\n* Turn real user language into copy, case studies, and testimonials.\n\n* Experiment with basic growth loops (invites, sharing, referrals) in lightweight ways.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Identify emergent behaviours and “weird” use cases that keep showing up.\n\n* Decide if you’re seeing early product‑market fit or just noisy enthusiasm.\n\n* Be willing to adjust positioning or roadmap based on what actually works, not what was planned.\n\n---\n\n## **6\\. Distillation – Refine and systematize**\n\n**Definition**  \n You repeatedly “boil off” what doesn’t matter and keep the essence: clean up the product, processes, and messaging using data and experience. This is where you get serious about quality and repeatability.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Refactor core code; pay down high‑interest tech debt.\n\n* Harden performance, reliability, and security; add automated test coverage.\n\n* Standardize patterns, libraries, and conventions across teams.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Build regular cadences: OKRs, roadmap reviews, incident/post‑mortem reviews.\n\n* Improve and automate recurring workflows (deploys, billing, renewals).\n\n* Use dashboards/metrics to drive decisions, not just anecdotes.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Double down on channels with proven CAC/LTV; prune the rest.\n\n* Optimize funnel steps (activation, onboarding, expansion) with experimentation.\n\n* Develop brand and style guidelines so assets feel consistent.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Define clear product‑market fit indicators and monitor them.\n\n* Tighten focus on the core value loop—what users do that drives durable value.\n\n* Codify “playbooks” for acquisition, onboarding, and expansion so others can run them.\n\n---\n\n## **7\\. Coagulation – Solidify into a durable product & platform**\n\n**Definition**  \n The refined essence “sets” into a stable form: a robust product, brand, and operating model. This becomes the new baseline—until the next cycle begins.\n\n**Software dev / implementation**\n\n* Establish predictable release trains and versioning (LTS, breaking‑change policy).\n\n* Define platform boundaries and public APIs/SDKs for partners and integrations.\n\n* Make conscious tradeoffs toward stability over rapid change in core surfaces.\n\n**Business practices / operations**\n\n* Formalize org structure, roles, and decision authorities around the product.\n\n* Build governance for security, privacy, compliance, and risk.\n\n* Lock in budgets, capacity planning, and hiring plans aligned with the product’s role.\n\n**Marketing & growth**\n\n* Clarify long‑term positioning and category narrative; aim for leadership, not just participation.\n\n* Invest in durable assets: documentation, education, community, partnerships.\n\n* Run larger‑scale campaigns and PR with a stable, recognizable brand.\n\n**Product strategy & evolution**\n\n* Decide which moats you are compounding (ecosystem, data, distribution, brand).\n\n* Spin out new product lines or major bets on top of the “coagulated” platform.\n\n* Start a *new* alchemical cycle for the next big initiative—burning down assumptions again at a higher level.\n\n---\n\n**Hermetic maxim:**  \n *As you refine the product, you refine the team; as above in vision, so below in code and practice.*\n\n",
    "106c50bb2e06702c1c72764ccece3d5c500bddf4b553e12afa0c4d1f8c7a4c21": "\n\n# **PF13-Reference-Glow Development Philosophy v1** \n\n## **A. Intent and audience**\n\n**Purpose.** Guide AI sessions to plan EPICs, choose strategies, prevent drift, and move fast through controlled change.\n\n**Audience.** AI agents that design or execute work at Glow.\n\n**Scope.** Values, lenses, decision rubrics, tension guides, glossary, and a small machine-readable annex with stable keys only.\n\n**Non-scope.** Procedures, steps, file paths, schemas, APIs, headers, tokens, environment variables, tools, team workflows, acceptance matrices, or examples tied to any specific project or stack.\n\n**Routing rule.** When methods or specifications are needed, refer by category only: Process Guide, Architecture, Transport, Infrastructure, Security and Privacy, Data and ML, Testing and Quality.\n\n**Non-redundancy and stability.** PF13 changes rarely. Edit only when a tenet changes meaning, category names change, or an elemental lens is added or retired. Before editing, apply these guard tests: the change alters philosophy rather than process; it avoids duplicating material that belongs in a category home; it remains true across projects and stacks.\n\n**AI usage contract.** At the start or revision of an EPIC, AI sessions must 1\\) read PF13, 2\\) use the four elements as lenses for strategy, and 3\\) emit the EPIC Strategy Card described later. PF13 is the source of truth for philosophy only. All methods and proofs live in their category homes.\n\n## **B. Core tenets**\n\n### **1\\) Controlled change enables speed**\n\n**What this means.** We move fast by shaping work into clear, verifiable changes that reduce rework. Speed comes from control, not from skipping steps.  \n **AI behaviors.** State the outcome in one paragraph, choose a batch size that proves it quickly, finish before starting something else, and include an explicit verify step.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Is the intent legible in one paragraph? Will this slice prove value quickly? What must be true to call it verified?\n\n### **2\\) Single home per concept**\n\n**What this means.** Every concept has one authoritative home. Other texts point to it rather than copy it.  \n **AI behaviors.** When you need a fact or rule, point readers to the home by category. If a new concept appears, propose a home before spreading details across documents.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Are we duplicating content that already has a home? If a new idea emerged, did we name its home?\n\n### **3\\) Coherent public surfaces**\n\n**What this means.** There is one calm place where truth is observed. Interfaces stay simple and human. Internals remain private.  \n **AI behaviors.** Prefer one published surface per concept, keep public contracts minimal, and avoid leaking internal scaffolding. Treat reads as confirmation of reality.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Did we create a second surface for the same idea? Does the interface expose internals?\n\n### **4\\) Clear boundaries with versioned evolution**\n\n**What this means.** Name the contract first, then change the implementation behind it. Evolve by adding versions instead of breaking agreements.  \n **AI behaviors.** Separate public surface, application logic, and core ideas. Use explicit, programmatic configuration. Allow old and new to coexist during migration.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Is there a named contract? Can versions coexist safely? Is configuration explicit rather than hidden flags?\n\n### **5\\) Professionalism and stewardship**\n\n**What this means.** Respect people and future readers. Favor privacy, least privilege, and legible intent.  \n **AI behaviors.** Minimize data collected, design observability that identifies events without exposing secrets, and write decisions so they are understandable later.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Are we collecting only what is needed? Would leaked logs cause harm? Can a future reader see why we chose this?\n\n### **6\\) Phase discipline and verification before scale**\n\n**What this means.** Work flows through lightweight phases: intent, scope, design, implement, verify, release, learn. Verification precedes scale.  \n **AI behaviors.** Declare entry and exit signals for each phase, keep work visible, and never skip verification to gain speed.  \n **Anti-drift checks.** Are phase boundaries clear? Is there a concrete verify step and success signal before release?\n\n## **C. The four elements**\n\n### **1\\) FIRE — Truth (effectiveness and momentum)**\n\n**Aim.** Make a specific truth real fast, with proof.  \n **AI must emit before work begins.**\n\n* **Outcome (one sentence):** “After this change, **X is true**.”  \n* **Success signal:** the smallest observable that proves X (metric, log key, state check).  \n* **Scope line:** what is in and out for this cut.\n\n**Design rules.**\n\n* Choose the **smallest implementation** that makes X true without side quests.  \n* Keep one owner and one intent for the cut.  \n* Prefer clarity over cleverness.\n\n**Developer moves.**\n\n* Name the user or system effect, not the technique.  \n* Wire a **single observation** that proves X happened.  \n* Finish and stabilize before starting anything adjacent.\n\n**Fast proof and exit.**\n\n* Show the observation once in a controlled run.  \n* Record the one-paragraph intent and result.  \n* Declare what the next increment would be.\n\n**Anti-patterns to avoid.**\n\n* Multi-intent bundles, vague outcomes, “we’ll verify later.”  \n  ---\n\n  ### **2\\) WATER — Love & Integrity (coherence and consistency)**\n\n**Aim.** Honor relationships. Keep one calm surface people can trust.  \n **AI must emit before work begins.**\n\n* **Surface statement:** name the single public surface this change touches.  \n* **Promise check:** what existing promise must remain true.  \n* **Minimal contract phrase:** plain words for what the surface will now express.\n\n**Design rules.**\n\n* One **home per concept**. Point to it; do not copy.  \n* Public contracts are **humane and minimal**. Internals stay private.  \n* Reads confirm reality. Writes are gentle and do not claim to be truth.\n\n**Developer moves.**\n\n* Remove duplicate public faces for the same idea.  \n* Trim internal numerics or scaffolding from public messages.  \n* Keep terminology consistent with prior promises.\n\n**Fast proof and exit.**\n\n* Demonstrate the surface shows the expected truth in one place only.  \n* Show that older clients or readers still understand the message.\n\n**Anti-patterns to avoid.**\n\n* Second surfaces, leaky abstractions, novelty that breaks consistency.  \n  ---\n\n  ### **3\\) AIR — Knowledge & Data (boundaries and evolution)**\n\n**Aim.** Decide with knowledge, design clear boundaries, evolve by version.  \n **AI must emit before work begins.**\n\n* **Contract name:** what agreement defines this change.  \n* **Evolution plan:** add a version or additive field rather than break in place.  \n* **Data posture:** the minimum data needed and how it is observed.\n\n**Design rules.**\n\n* **Contracts first.** Implementation follows behind the boundary.  \n* **Version forward.** Old and new can coexist. Plan the coexistence period.  \n* **Programmatic configuration.** No hidden flags or magic defaults.  \n* **Data minimalism.** Collect only what supports decisions and proofs.\n\n**Developer moves.**\n\n* Introduce a versioned seam instead of rewriting a live contract.  \n* Make configuration explicit and typed.  \n* Separate core logic from time, IO, and concurrency concerns.\n\n**Fast proof and exit.**\n\n* Show old and new behaviors running side-by-side without conflict.  \n* Show rollback is one move that restores prior behavior.\n\n**Anti-patterns to avoid.**\n\n* Hidden cross-layer coupling, flag sprawl, rollbacks that require rewrites.  \n  ---\n\n  ### **4\\) EARTH — Foundation (everything comes together)**\n\n**Aim.** Land the change on solid ground that is safe, understandable, and durable.  \n **AI must emit before work begins.**\n\n* **Ownership:** who is responsible for this change.  \n* **Phase signals:** entry condition, exit condition, and handoff target.  \n* **Safety note:** the failure mode and why it is acceptable.\n\n**Design rules.**\n\n* Least privilege. Observability without exposing secrets.  \n* Clear ownership and continuity. The future reader can follow the why.  \n* Resilience first. Degraded behavior is intentional and safe.\n\n**Developer moves.**\n\n* Write the one-paragraph “why” where future readers will look.  \n* Choose defaults that fail closed and recover cleanly.  \n* Prove the change works in an environment that resembles reality.\n\n**Fast proof and exit.**\n\n* Demonstrate the happy path once and the failure path once.  \n* Show that failure leaves the system coherent and recoverable.\n\n**Anti-patterns to avoid.**\n\n* Over-collection of data, logs that reveal payloads, irreversible migrations.  \n  ---\n\n  ### **How you apply this in development (one pass per element, fast)**\n\n* **Start with FIRE:** write the one-sentence outcome, success signal, and scope line.  \n* **Check WATER:** confirm the single public surface and restate the promise that must hold.  \n* **Define AIR:** name the contract, state the version step, and the minimum data you will observe.  \n* **Anchor EARTH:** name ownership, entry/exit signals, and the acceptable failure mode.\n\nIf any element fails its fast proof, stop and adjust there before proceeding.\n\n## **D. Alchemical delivery cycle**\n\n> Seven lightweight phases that let AI sessions move fast through **controlled change**. For each phase, capture only: **purpose**, **entry signal**, **exit signal**, **handoff**. No steps or checklists live in PF13.\n\n### **1\\) Intent**\n\n* **Purpose.** State the single **truth** we will make real and why it matters.  \n* **Entry signal.** A clear problem/opportunity and the audience who cares.  \n* **Exit signal.** One-sentence outcome and success signal agreed.  \n* **Handoff.** Pass the outcome and success signal to **Scope**.\n\n  ### **2\\) Scope**\n\n* **Purpose.** Set **boundaries** and batch size; decide what’s in/out for this cut.  \n* **Entry signal.** Accepted outcome \\+ any hard constraints or assumptions.  \n* **Exit signal.** Crisp “in/out” list, target surface named, risks acknowledged.  \n* **Handoff.** Provide constraints, target surface, and risks to **Design**.\n\n  ### **3\\) Design**\n\n* **Purpose.** Choose the approach that satisfies the outcome while preserving **coherence**, **data minimalism**, and a **versioned** path forward.  \n* **Entry signal.** Scoped constraints, target surface, and quality bar.  \n* **Exit signal.** Named contract, version/evolution note, minimal data to observe, and stated failure mode.  \n* **Handoff.** Deliver the design record (contract, version, observables, failure note) to **Implement**.\n\n  ### **4\\) Implement**\n\n* **Purpose.** Make the change real with the smallest construction that meets the design; keep ownership singular.  \n* **Entry signal.** Accepted design record and a representative environment to run in.  \n* **Exit signal.** Working change with the success signal wired, safe defaults chosen, and intent recorded in one paragraph.  \n* **Handoff.** Provide the running change and observation instructions to **Verify**.\n\n  ### **5\\) Verify**\n\n* **Purpose.** Prove the change achieved the intended **truth** and did not create drift.  \n* **Entry signal.** Deployed change \\+ ready observables.  \n* **Exit signal.** Evidence shows the success signal; coherence preserved; rollback remains one move.  \n* **Handoff.** Share a short verification note and approvals to **Release**.\n\n  ### **6\\) Release**\n\n* **Purpose.** Make the promise **durable and visible** without creating new surfaces; keep reversibility.  \n* **Entry signal.** Verified change and go-live approval.  \n* **Exit signal.** Promise live; ownership and reversibility documented; communications delivered where they belong.  \n* **Handoff.** Provide outcomes and any follow-ups to **Learn**.\n\n  ### **7\\) Learn**\n\n* **Purpose.** Capture insights and remove waste to accelerate the next cycle.  \n* **Entry signal.** Post-release data and stakeholder feedback.  \n* **Exit signal.** Succinct learning notes, next increment decision, and any corrections to language or heuristics.  \n* **Handoff.** Begin the next **Intent** with updated understanding.\n\n## **E. Working nimble without waste**\n\n### **1\\) Define outcomes in plain language *(FIRE: truth)***\n\n**Principle.** Say exactly what will be true when you are done. Plain words create speed.  \n **Decision prompts.** Is the outcome specific, falsifiable, and meaningful to the people who care? Does it avoid technique words? Could a skeptical reader tell if it happened?  \n **Red flags.** Vague verbs (improve, optimize), stacked goals in one sentence, success that depends on unspoken conditions.\n\n### **2\\) Choose batch size that proves value fast *(AIR: knowledge, WATER: integrity)***\n\n**Principle.** Ship a slice that demonstrates value without pulling in side concerns.  \n **Decision prompts.** What is the smallest change that would convince a reasonable reviewer? What can be safely deferred without corrupting the result? Does the slice have one intent and one place it shows up?  \n **Red flags.** Scope creep, attaching “quick extras,” slices that only make sense if several other things land at the same time.\n\n### **3\\) Limit WIP and finish slices *(EARTH: foundation, FIRE: truth)***\n\n**Principle.** Flow beats multitasking. Finished work teaches and reduces risk.  \n **Decision prompts.** How many things are truly in progress right now? What is blocking the oldest slice, and is that blockade explicit? Does the next action directly move the current slice to finished?  \n **Red flags.** Two or more active slices touching the same surface, “nearly done” items aging without a clear blocker, new work starting before closure.\n\n### **4\\) Prefer proofs over narrative *(AIR: knowledge, WATER: integrity)***\n\n**Principle.** Evidence ends debate. Stories follow facts.  \n **Decision prompts.** What simple observation would show the outcome happened? Can another reader repeat that observation without inside knowledge? Does the observation check what matters rather than a side effect?  \n **Red flags.** Long explanations without a crisp observation, proofs that rely on internals, success declared without something observable.\n\n## **F. Drift prevention and double-checking**\n\n**Goal.** No orphaned code, no duplicate truths, no undocumented behavior. Every meaningful change is traceable as **Intent → Change → Proof**, bound to a single home.\n\n### **1\\) Single home rule for concepts *(WATER · EARTH)***\n\n**Principle.** Each concept has one authoritative home; everything else points to it.  \n **How this prevents drift.** A change that cannot be named to its home **cannot disappear**—it is either attached or it doesn’t ship.  \n **Decision prompts.** What is the concept’s home? If the change implies a new concept, what will its home be? Does any sentence in this work duplicate a truth that already has a home?  \n **Red flags.** New terms introduced with no home; two documents describing the same truth; “temporary” write-ups that become de facto sources.\n\n### **2\\) Titles-only cross references between documents *(WATER · AIR)***\n\n**Principle.** Reference by **category/title only**; never restate the content.  \n **How this prevents drift.** When the source changes, nothing else needs updating—no copied text to rot.  \n **Decision prompts.** Are we pointing to the home, or are we restating it here? Does this sentence force a second place to maintain the same idea?  \n **Red flags.** Pasted definitions; parallel “summaries” that diverge; examples that quietly become normative text.\n\n### **3\\) Two-pass check: author intent, then reader inference *(FIRE · AIR)***\n\n**Principle.** The maker states the intent; an independent reader (or AI session) re-states what the change **actually** does. Both must match.  \n **How this prevents drift.** Catching mismatch early stops code from shipping with a different truth than the one documented.  \n **Decision prompts.** If a skeptical reader saw only the change and its public effects, would they infer the same outcome sentence? Can the change be mistaken for a different promise?  \n **Red flags.** Intent that can be read two ways; change that alters semantics beyond what the intent claims; “it’s obvious from the code.”\n\n### **4\\) Evidence and its index updated together, at the source home only *(AIR · EARTH)***\n\n**Principle.** **Proof** (what shows the change happened) and the **index entry** that names that proof move as one, and **only** in the home that owns the concept.  \n **How this prevents drift.** No orphan proofs; no indexes pointing to nowhere; no duplicate indexes to forget later.  \n **Decision prompts.** Where does the owning home list proofs for this concept? Does this change add or retire a proof there? Is any other place trying to track the same proof?  \n **Red flags.** “We’ll update the index later”; evidence stored away from its owning home; more than one index tracking the same thing.\n\n---\n\n## **G. Alignment to EPICs (stay in frame)**\n\n**Directive.** For delivery, **adhere to the Epic process as documented in the Process Guide**. PF13 does not restate or modify that process.\n\n**AI discipline to prevent drift (no process, just guardrails):**\n\n* **Read before write.** Consult the category homes (Process, Architecture, Transport, Infrastructure, Security & Privacy, Data & ML, Testing & Quality). If something’s missing, ask the **smallest** clarifying question.  \n* **No embellishment.** Do not invent paths, fields, tokens, schemas, or “helper” surfaces. If it isn’t in the docs, don’t create it.  \n* **Single home only.** Every concept is bound to **one** home; point to it by category. If a new concept appears, propose a home (category) rather than scattering details.  \n* **Titles-only routing.** Refer by category titles, not document text; never copy definitions across docs.  \n* **No second surface.** Do not add a new public surface for an existing truth. If a change implies one, pause and escalate.  \n* **Match intent to observable behavior.** Keep the stated outcome and what is observable in alignment; if they diverge, stop and reconcile.  \n* **Contradictions → halt.** When docs conflict, stop work and pinpoint the conflict for adjudication. No “best guesses.”\n\nNot process. Section H is a **decision lens** you use when options are close, so choices stay consistent and drift-free without prescribing steps.\n\n## **H. Tension guides and decision rubric**\n\n### **Purpose**\n\nResolve tough choices quickly and consistently using the four elements as a lens. No steps, no checklists. This is a tie-breaker, not a procedure.\n\n### **Tie-breakers**\n\n* **FIRE (truth) vs speed.** Prefer the option that makes a specific truth plainly real and provable now. If speed risks muddy truth, choose truth.  \n* **WATER (love/integrity) vs breadth.** Prefer coherence of the single public surface over adding more capability that fractures it.  \n* **AIR (knowledge/data) vs quick fix.** Prefer a clear contract and additive version path over a patch that hides coupling or blocks rollback.  \n* **EARTH (foundation) vs convenience.** Prefer the safer failure shape, clearer ownership, and future legibility over shortcuts that increase risk.\n\n  ### **Simple four-lens scoring (1–5)**\n\nScore each option on FIRE, WATER, AIR, EARTH. Keep it quick and qualitative.\n\n* **FIRE (truth).** 1 \\= outcome vague or unprovable. 5 \\= outcome crisp, observable now.  \n* **WATER (integrity).** 1 \\= fragments the surface or leaks internals. 5 \\= keeps one calm surface, honors prior promises.  \n* **AIR (knowledge).** 1 \\= hidden coupling, breakage risk, data bloat. 5 \\= named contract, additive version, minimal necessary data.  \n* **EARTH (foundation).** 1 \\= unclear ownership, unsafe failure, hard to understand later. 5 \\= clear owner, safe failure, legible intent.\n\nAdd the four numbers. Use it to focus the discussion, not to mechanize it.\n\n### **Tie resolution rule**\n\nIf totals tie, pick the option with:\n\n1. **safer reversibility**, then  \n2. **clearer ownership**, then  \n3. **fewer public surfaces or flags**.\n\nIf still tied, prefer the option that reduces future choices rather than multiplying them.\n\n### **Why this prevents drift**\n\n* It anchors every decision to truth, surface coherence, explicit contracts, and safe foundations.  \n* It blocks “quick fixes” that create second surfaces, silent contract changes, or undocumented behavior.  \n* It keeps AI sessions inside the frame: adhere to procedure elsewhere, apply this lens to choose well.\n\n## **I. Definition of done (philosophical)**\n\n> A change is **done** when these element-truths hold. This is a lens, not a procedure.\n\n### **1\\) FIRE — Outcome is clear and matched by the change (truth)**\n\n**Principle.** The promised truth is now real and plainly observable.  \n **Decision prompts.** Would a skeptical reader state the same outcome after seeing the result? Does any part of the change claim more than the outcome?  \n **Red flags.** Vague outcome, side-effects presented as success, multiple outcomes hiding in one change.\n\n### **2\\) WATER — No second surface created (love / integrity)**\n\n**Principle.** There remains **one** calm public surface for this truth; prior promises still hold.  \n **Decision prompts.** Did we add or imply another place for users or systems to look? Did we leak internals into the public face?  \n **Red flags.** Duplicate interfaces, renamed concepts without continuity, “temporary” surfaces that become permanent.\n\n### **3\\) AIR — Boundaries respected and versioned (knowledge / data)**\n\n**Principle.** Contracts are named; evolution is **additive** and reversible; knowledge captured is minimal and relevant.  \n **Decision prompts.** Which contract did we change, and how is the path forward versioned? Can old and new coexist without guesswork? Are we storing only what supports decisions?  \n **Red flags.** Hidden coupling across layers, breaking changes in place, flag sprawl, data collected “just in case.”\n\n### **4\\) EARTH — Stewardship evident; learning captured (foundation)**\n\n**Principle.** The change is safe, legible, and leaves the system whole; what we learned will guide the next cut.  \n **Decision prompts.** Does this fail safely? Can a future reader understand the why in a paragraph? What did we learn that materially shapes the next move?  \n **Red flags.** Risk moved to users, logs that expose secrets, outcomes that can’t be understood later, no takeaway for the next iteration.\n\n* ## **J. Glossary**\n\n* **Controlled change** *(FIRE · EARTH)*  \n   A way of working where each change has a single, stated truth to make real and a clear boundary around it. It accelerates delivery by reducing rework and surprise.  \n   Anti-drift focus: if the truth cannot be stated plainly, the change is not ready.  \n* **Single home** *(WATER)*  \n   The one authoritative place a concept lives. All other texts point to it rather than restating it.  \n   Anti-drift focus: if a fact appears in two places, one of them is wrong.  \n* **Calm surface** *(WATER)*  \n   The single coherent public face where reality is observed. It is plain, minimal, and stable; internals remain private.  \n   Anti-drift focus: do not create a second surface for the same idea.  \n* **Deterministic core (as an idea)** *(AIR)*  \n   Logic that gives the same output for the same inputs, with uncertainty and side effects kept at the edges. This is a design stance, not a stack choice.  \n   Anti-drift focus: if results vary without input change, the core is leaking outside influence.  \n* **Programmatic configuration** *(AIR)*  \n   Behavior controlled by explicit, typed, versioned inputs rather than hidden flags or guesses.  \n   Anti-drift focus: if behavior changes without an intentional input change, configuration is not truly programmatic.  \n* **Drift** *(FIRE · WATER · AIR · EARTH)*  \n   Any divergence between intended truth, public surface, named contract, and observable reality. It includes orphan code, duplicate truths, and undocumented changes.  \n   Anti-drift focus: every meaningful change binds to a home, a stated outcome, and a way to observe it.  \n* **Versioned evolution** *(AIR)*  \n   Changing agreements by adding versions or additive fields so old and new can coexist. No breaking in place.  \n   Anti-drift focus: if consumers must guess or break to keep up, evolution was not truly versioned.\n\nK. Machine-readable annex\n\nStable constants for AI ingestion. Keys only. No IDs, paths, tokens, or project specifics.\n\n{\n\n  \"pf13\\_annex\": {\n\n    \"audience\": \"AI-only\",\n\n    \"tenets\": \\[\n\n      \"controlled\\_change\",\n\n      \"single\\_home\",\n\n      \"coherent\\_surface\",\n\n      \"clear\\_boundaries\\_versioned\",\n\n      \"stewardship\",\n\n      \"phase\\_discipline\\_verification\"\n\n    \\],\n\n    \"elements\": {\n\n      \"FIRE\": { \"label\": \"truth\", \"prompts\": \\[\"outcome\", \"success\\_signal\", \"scope\\_line\"\\] },\n\n      \"WATER\": { \"label\": \"love\\_integrity\", \"prompts\": \\[\"surface\", \"promise\\_check\"\\] },\n\n      \"AIR\": { \"label\": \"knowledge\\_data\", \"prompts\": \\[\"contract\", \"version\\_path\", \"data\\_minimum\"\\] },\n\n      \"EARTH\": { \"label\": \"foundation\", \"prompts\": \\[\"ownership\", \"fail\\_safe\", \"legibility\"\\] }\n\n    },\n\n    \"strategy\\_card\\_fields\": \\[\n\n      \"outcome\\_fire\",\n\n      \"surface\\_water\",\n\n      \"boundary\\_air\",\n\n      \"stewardship\\_earth\"\n\n    \\],\n\n    \"rubric\\_fields\": \\[\"FIRE\", \"WATER\", \"AIR\", \"EARTH\"\\],\n\n    \"tie\\_breaker\\_rule\": \"prefer\\_option\\_with\\_safer\\_reversibility\\_then\\_clearer\\_ownership\"\n\n  }\n\n}\n\n## **L. Stewardship of PF13**\n\n**Reference only, low change rate.** PF13 is philosophy for AI sessions. It should be stable and sparse. Treat it as a compass, not a playbook.\n\n**Rare update triggers (the only reasons to edit PF13):**\n\n1. A **tenet** changes in meaning.  \n2. The set or names of **category homes** change (Process, Architecture, Transport, Infrastructure, Security and Privacy, Data and ML, Testing and Quality).  \n3. An elemental **lens** is added or retired (FIRE, WATER, AIR, EARTH) or their mappings shift (truth, love/integrity, knowledge/data, foundation).\n\n**Immutables.**\n\n* Audience \\= **AI only**.  \n* Scope \\= **philosophy and lenses**; Non-scope \\= **procedures, paths, schemas, APIs, tokens, tools, examples tied to a project**.  \n* **Titles-only** routing to category homes; no duplication.  \n* Machine-readable annex \\= **stable keys only**.\n\n**Change guards (must all be true before any edit):**\n\n* The edit adjusts **philosophy**, not process or examples.  \n* It **does not duplicate** content that lives in a category home.  \n* It remains **true across projects and stacks**.\n\nIf a proposed change fails any guard, do not edit PF13; update or create the relevant category document instead.\n\n",
    "30540aaf33501c1e24a9d380a5b45ac7e832bfc729bb56ca71ff7ff1e2947571": "---\nname: flowmaster-primary\ndescription: Orchestrate a user-specified, multi-session ChatGPT workflow with durable state, one-way send locks, exact session identity, bounded recovery, and terminal-result validation. Use for a generic Flowmaster run or for maintaining the canonical Flowmaster core. Do not use in place of an installed domain specialization such as tw-flowmaster or change-flow when that specialization applies.\n---\n\n# Flowmaster Primary\n\nUse this skill directly only for a genuinely generic orchestration request whose domain stages and outputs are completely supplied by the user. For Technical Writing or Change Flow execution, invoke the corresponding self-contained specialization instead; do not invoke Primary alongside it.\n\nPrimary is the canonical maintenance source for the embedded Flowmaster core. Runtime specializations contain a complete copy of the marked core block and do not load or call this skill. A Primary update therefore changes no specialization until the core is explicitly propagated and validated.\n\nFor a direct generic run, require the governing flow specification to establish roles, sources, stages, dependencies, authorizations, outputs, success predicates, and final reporting. Apply the core below without inventing missing domain behavior.\n\n<!-- FLOWMASTER_CORE_BEGIN -->\n## Flowmaster core contract\n\n`FLOWMASTER_CORE_REVISION: 1.0.2`\n\n### Operating posture\n\n- Act as the controller and evidence keeper, not as a substitute for the worker sessions being orchestrated.\n- Execute external sends, writes, session creation, or configuration only when the user has asked to run or continue the flow and the governing specialization authorizes that action.\n- For an explanation, review, audit, RCA, design, or plan, remain read-only.\n- Never infer that permission for one flow, session, source, or mutation authorizes another.\n- Treat an unavailable capability, authentication gate, permission denial, CAPTCHA, ambiguous identity, or authority conflict as a stop condition. Request only the smallest necessary operator action.\n- Do not claim downstream completion from dispatch, startup, elapsed time, an artifact name, or an unverified link.\n\n### External confirmation checkpoints\n\nWorkflow authorization and a control-layer action-time confirmation are separate. A required checkpoint does not mean the operator's prior instruction was missing, unclear, or invalid.\n\n- Determine from the active control layer whether the exact imminent action requires a checkpoint. Do not assume that every browser or external action always requires one.\n- Prepare the transaction as far as the active policy permits, then request confirmation at the latest permitted moment. State that the prior instruction remains valid and identify the exact operation, destination, payload, and asset scope.\n- Bind a granted checkpoint to a confirmation action key containing the action key, target or destination, payload identity or hash, asset identities, and composer checksum. Any material change invalidates the grant; unchanged re-verification does not require another checkpoint.\n- Group checkpoints only when the active control layer permits it and every grouped action is imminent and fully specified. Never preconfirm an unknown future response, payload, destination, or generated relay turn.\n- Confirmation is not a send attempt. A request, grant, decline, or invalidation must not set `SEND_ATTEMPTED`, create a dispatch lock, or be counted as a send.\n- After a valid grant, reverify the exact destination and composer checksum, attempt the action exactly once, and only then apply the one-way send lock.\n\n### Authority and complete sources\n\nApply authority in this order unless the specialization establishes a stricter order:\n\n1. Current system instructions and the operator's latest explicit instruction for this run.\n2. The active self-contained specialization or, for a direct generic run, this skill.\n3. The validated run manifest and scoped operator note.\n4. The exact stage prompt, limited to its declared task.\n5. The current authoritative source or artifact designated for that stage.\n6. Directly observed session history and external state.\n7. The run ledger as a checkpoint only, never as independent proof.\n\nRead every decisive prompt, source, turn, and artifact as the complete required unit. A preview, snippet, search hit, summary, filename, ellipsis, cutoff, or content ending mid-unit is incomplete. Stop relying on incomplete retrieval, recover within the bounded-recovery rule, and redo dependent analysis after recovery. Retrieval failure is not evidence that content is absent.\n\nPin mutable stage prompts at first use by exact identity and complete content. If the same identity later resolves to materially different content and the pinned copy is unavailable, stop under prompt drift rather than silently switching versions.\n\n### Run mode and identity\n\nUse exactly one run mode:\n\n- `FRESH`: create a new ledger; do not retrieve prior Flowmaster conversations, broad personal context, or an older run ledger. Inspect existing worker-session history only for current operational facts needed for identity, duplicate prevention, capability state, and active work.\n- `RESUME`: recover only the exact retained ledger and exact session identities for the named run. Reconcile them against live sources before any new action. Do not perform broad historical reconstruction.\n\nDefault to `FRESH` only when the specialization permits a default; otherwise require the field. Derive a stable run identity from the supplied flow name or explicit run key. Never merge two runs because their names or targets resemble one another.\n\n### Separated state model\n\nTrack these layers independently for every managed session or target:\n\n- controller health;\n- tab ownership and visibility;\n- session identity and configuration;\n- composer state;\n- send state;\n- assistant-turn state;\n- source or artifact validation state;\n- task outcome; and\n- tab-close lease.\n\nDo not collapse controller failure into task failure, session invisibility into session absence, an empty text field into an empty composer, a send timeout into a failed send, or assistant startup into task completion.\n\nUse a one-way stage state machine:\n\n1. `SESSION_UNRESOLVED`\n2. `SESSION_VISIBLE_IDLE`\n3. `COMPOSER_READY`\n4. `SEND_ATTEMPTED`\n5. `DELIVERY_UNKNOWN_OR_RECONCILING`\n6. `DELIVERY_RECONCILED`\n7. `TURN_NOT_REQUIRED` only when the specialization explicitly declares a no-response endpoint, otherwise `TURN_UNKNOWN_OR_RUNNING`\n8. `TURN_TERMINAL` when a response is required\n9. `RESULT_VALIDATED` or `RESULT_BLOCKED`\n\nAfter `SEND_ATTEMPTED`, no transition returns to composition unless positive read-only evidence proves that no message was sent and the corrected-attempt rule permits one retry.\n\nBefore sending, pin the exact destination-history or external-state baseline needed to distinguish this action from any pre-existing identical effect. After the send attempt, establish `DELIVERY_RECONCILED` only from one new action-bound effect after that baseline. Unless the specialization explicitly declares that no assistant response is required, continue through the assistant-turn states. A no-response endpoint validates transport or delivery only and must never imply assistant startup, task acceptance, or downstream work completion.\n\n### Durable ledger and action identity\n\nMaintain compact current-run state. Use a durable ledger when the flow has multiple targets, spans multiple sessions or stages, resumes, encounters an ambiguous action or controller reset, or otherwise risks losing exact state.\n\nRecord only what is needed to resume safely:\n\n- run and manifest identity;\n- pinned prompt identities and content hashes;\n- authoritative source identities and versions;\n- session titles, stable session identifiers, and tab mappings;\n- configuration and session-scoped capability states;\n- stage, target, cycle, and dependency states;\n- composer checksum and dispatch identity;\n- pre-action destination baseline, delivery state, and exact new delivery-evidence identity;\n- response requirement and assistant-turn state;\n- confirmation requirement, confirmation action key, and outcome when applicable;\n- send, turn, validation, terminal, recovery, and cleanup states;\n- last confirmed action and next permitted action.\n\nDo not copy complete prompts, source documents, output artifacts, credentials, signed URLs, or unsupported conclusions into the ledger. Write a transition only after the corresponding state is directly verified.\n\nBefore any external send or write, form an action key from the run, stage, target or cycle, session, prompt identity, input identities and versions, and intended operation. Check both the ledger and live destination. If the action or its effect is already confirmed, do not repeat it.\n\n### Browser, tab, and session ownership\n\n- Inventory tabs before browser work without opening or inspecting the executing Flowmaster session.\n- Leave every pre-existing tab untouched. Never refresh, repurpose, navigate away from, or close a tab the flow did not open.\n- Use exactly one flow-owned tab per managed ChatGPT session and retain an exact tab-to-session mapping.\n- Verify the active site, project or workspace, exact session title, and stable session identity immediately before every state-changing action.\n- Never browser-open, inspect, configure, message, or verify the current executing Flowmaster session.\n- Do not assume a session-creation API exists. Use only currently available, authorized ChatGPT controls and verify the created session's type, project placement, title, and stable identity before configuration or work.\n- Prefer an existing authoritative session when the specialization permits it. Never create a replacement to escape controller-wide failure, an unresolved session set, or an ambiguous current-run send.\n\nSet `TAB_CLOSE_ALLOWED = false` whenever an active or possibly active turn still requires observation. Release the lease only after the specialization's required terminal result is visible, retrieved completely, checked, and checkpointed. Startup, elapsed time, controller unreadability, switching targets, or a stopped animation does not release it.\n\nClose each flow-owned tab when its required work is terminal and checked. Before final reporting or a flow-wide stop, attempt cleanup through every still-healthy route and report any tab whose closure could not be verified.\n\n### Control hierarchy\n\nUse the safest semantic control available:\n\n1. direct connector or structured control;\n2. exact URL or retained session identity;\n3. keyboard or inline command such as `/model` or an actual `@` picker selection;\n4. a semantic click when no safer route exists, including `Show in text field` or selecting an exact autocomplete result;\n5. coordinate-based interaction only when unavoidable and directly verifiable.\n\nVerify the resulting state. Do not press Enter to test focus or accept a suggestion unless the suggestion menu is visibly focused, because Enter may submit the composer.\n\nWhen a target-session task requires a ChatGPT skill, select the exact installed skill through the target composer's real `@` picker and verify the resulting skill chip before sending. Plain copied text that spells `@skill-name` is not sufficient evidence of activation. A skill active in the controlling session does not automatically carry into another session.\n\n### Composer transaction\n\nTreat the composer as one transaction across all visible surfaces: text field, prompt or file tiles, variable values, actual skill or connector chips, attachments or Library references, and session history.\n\nFor a long or stored prompt:\n\n1. Paste or insert the complete prompt exactly once.\n2. If ChatGPT converts it to a tile, use `Show in text field` once when available.\n3. Populate only declared variables with exact values.\n4. Select every required actual skill, connector, or Library reference through its supported picker.\n5. Verify all surfaces together: one prompt copy, no unresolved required placeholder, exact values, exact references, exact chips, correct target session, and no equivalent message already in history.\n6. Record a compact composer checksum containing the target, session, prompt identity, input identities, selected skills or connectors, and model/reasoning state.\n7. Send once.\n\nIf `Show in text field` is unavailable, retain the single tile and add one short ordinary-message block containing only declared overrides:\n\n```text\nAUTHORITATIVE VARIABLE OVERRIDES FOR THE ATTACHED PROMPT\n<VARIABLE> = <exact value>\n\nTreat these values as replacing the corresponding unresolved variables in the attached prompt. Do not infer or substitute other values.\n```\n\nNever paste a second prompt copy merely because the text field appears empty. Never add undeclared substantive instructions through the override block.\n\n### One-way send lock\n\nImmediately before sending, verify that the session is idle, the composer checksum is correct, no equivalent dispatch exists, the stage dependency is satisfied, and any required action-time confirmation remains valid for the unchanged transaction.\n\nImmediately when the final send action is attempted:\n\n1. set `SEND_ATTEMPTED`;\n2. set the composer and session to write-locked;\n3. record the action key and time;\n4. leave the session immediately; and\n5. continue to the next independent ready item or begin the read-only monitoring cycle.\n\nDo not linger in the same composer to prove startup. A timeout, blank text field, missing immediate assistant text, redirect, browser reset, or slow response is never evidence that the send failed and never authorizes another paste, send, interrupt, replacement session, or correction message.\n\nPermit at most one corrected send, through a materially different route, only after positive read-only evidence proves all of the following:\n\n- no new action-bound matching user message or external effect exists after the exact pre-action baseline;\n- no assistant activity corresponds to the action;\n- the session is idle;\n- no staged prompt tile, composer content, or selected attachment or chip remains; and\n- the first send was not applied.\n\nIf any condition is unknown, preserve `SEND_STATE_UNKNOWN`, remain write-locked, and report a blocker.\n\n### Monitoring and scheduling\n\nAfter initial sends, reconcile delivery read-only, then use round-robin monitoring for every response that the specialization requires. A monitoring timeout limits only the observation operation, never model generation.\n\nAdvance independent work by readiness. Do not impose a batch-wide barrier when one target's next stage depends only on that target. Preserve source order for first dispatches, then process terminal results as they become ready. Keep operations serial when they share one writer, composer, living artifact, approval gate, or dependent session.\n\nDo not interrupt a running turn. Do not send a later stage into the same session while its prior turn is active. When a response is required, a turn is terminal only from direct visible terminal evidence defined by the specialization. When the specialization explicitly declares a no-response endpoint, do not inspect or characterize assistant-turn state as part of that endpoint.\n\n### Session-scoped capability state\n\nCache each required session-scoped capability as exactly one of:\n\n- `PRESENT`: direct history or UI evidence proves it was invoked or enabled;\n- `ABSENT`: direct inspection proves it has not been invoked or enabled; or\n- `UNKNOWN`: the state cannot be established.\n\nInvoke or enable the capability only from `ABSENT`, only when authorized, and at most once per session unless its governing integration explicitly requires another action. `PRESENT` persists across stages. `UNKNOWN` permits read-only recovery, not reinvocation.\n\n### Timeouts and bounded recovery\n\nApply a session-control timeout only to establishing that a page, tab, session, composer, or read-only state is visible and controllable. Never use it to time-limit assistant generation, source processing, or the entire flow.\n\nAfter any timeout or reported failure:\n\n1. treat the action's effect as unknown;\n2. perform read-only state inspection before another action;\n3. try no more than two materially different recovery routes after the initial failure;\n4. never repeat a failed route; and\n5. stop when the exact state is recovered or no permitted route remains.\n\nSuitable distinct routes include refreshing the same flow-owned tab and reopening the exact retained session by stable identity. If an exact-session reopen succeeds, replace the active mapping and close the superseded flow-owned tab when possible. Do not operate both mappings.\n\nDistinguish session-specific failure from controller-wide failure by using an independent safe tab or route for a non-mutating check. Controller-wide failure stops further sends; it does not prove that running turns failed and does not authorize replacement sessions.\n\n### Result validation and completion\n\nWhen the specialization requires an assistant response, validate the exact assistant turn and its complete final response against the active stage prompt and specialization. When the specialization explicitly declares a no-response endpoint, validate the exact new action-bound delivery evidence and every declared transport-only predicate instead; do not wait for, capture, or claim an assistant result. Retrieve and inspect every required output artifact through its authoritative source. A successful result requires every applicable success predicate, required artifact, required field, exact sentinel, and no-partial-package condition to pass.\n\nKeep the session write-locked and its tab lease active until the response or transport-only validation required by the specialization is complete. Record failure or blocker evidence exactly and do not advance a failed dependency.\n\nComplete the flow only when every identified work item has one terminal outcome, all required living artifacts and ledgers reconcile, every required approval or success predicate is verified, and flow-owned-tab cleanup has been attempted and reported. Completion means only the endpoint defined by the specialization. Delivery-only completion must be labeled as delivery or transport completion and never as completion of downstream work.\n\n### Blockers and reporting\n\nSeparate shared blockers from item-specific blockers. Continue independent items after a target-specific failure unless a shared indispensable source, controller, prompt, configuration, writer, or gate prevents safe work.\n\nFor every blocker retain:\n\n- run, stage, target or cycle, and session;\n- last confirmed action;\n- exact unknown, failure, or unmet predicate;\n- evidence available and missing;\n- recovery routes already attempted;\n- smallest operator action or input required; and\n- next safe action after resolution.\n\nUse distinct statuses for `NOT ATTEMPTED`, `SEND STATE UNKNOWN`, `DELIVERY STATE UNKNOWN`, `RUNNING`, `TERMINAL FAILED`, `TERMINAL BLOCKED`, and `TERMINAL SUCCESS`. Never use a startup blocker when no send was attempted, and never count an unknown or not-attempted dispatch as started or successful.\n\nBefore final output, reconcile every item exactly once, totals, approvals, artifact versions, active turns, ledger state, and tab cleanup. Use only the specialization's exact report contract and sentinel.\n<!-- FLOWMASTER_CORE_END -->\n\n## Direct generic execution\n\nFor a direct generic Flowmaster run:\n\n1. Validate a complete run specification and choose `FRESH` or `RESUME`.\n2. Derive the domain state machine and dependencies without weakening the embedded core.\n3. Inventory sources, sessions, tabs, capabilities, and authorized mutations.\n4. Execute sends under the composer transaction and one-way write lock.\n5.
